tldr: To keep an end-effector level while a quadruped robot walks on uneven terrain, the authors propose a hybrid representation (position relative to the base, orientation aligned with gravity) and reinforcement learning with a prioritized hierarchy (body posture > locomotion > manipulation). This enables stable operation on 30-degree slopes, stairs, and deformable ground.
hero_caption: System appearance and overview of challenges using a custom arm mounted on a compact quadruped robot (Unitree Go1). Even when disturbances from uneven terrain and center-of-mass shifts from arm movements heavily interfere with each other, the proposed method keeps the end-effector level while traversing steep slopes and stairs and performing manipulation tasks.
overview:
Quadruped manipulators—quadruped robots equipped with a robotic arm—are expected to inspect and work in environments with rubble and steps where wheeled robots cannot go. However, attempting manipulation while walking with an arm on a small-scale quadruped robot faces serious challenges. Moving the arm substantially shifts the entire robot's center of mass, and intense shaking from walking on uneven terrain travels directly to the end-effector. Particularly when carrying objects or using tools, any loss of end-effector orientation can be fatal, such as spilling contents.

To address this, the authors engineered the target representation of the end-effector and the reward structure of reinforcement learning. First, for end-effector commands, they devised a "hybrid task representation": specifying position relative to the robot's base (local) to avoid exceeding the arm's reachable workspace, while specifying orientation relative to the direction of gravity (global) so that it remains unaffected by ground slopes. Furthermore, in robot behavior learning, they introduced "task-prioritized learning" with an explicit priority: first maintain an upright body posture to prevent falls, next ensure reliable locomotion, and finally track end-effector targets. When walking becomes unstable, the policy avoids forcing end-effector tracking. Additionally, they built a custom ultra-lightweight 6-DoF arm weighing just 1.5 kg to reduce the weight burden.

The policy was trained via large-scale parallel reinforcement learning in a simulator (Isaac Lab) and transferred directly to real hardware (Unitree Go1) for validation. As a result, the robot demonstrated traversing steep slopes up to 30 degrees, stairs, and deformable terrain made of sponges and sandbags while keeping the end-effector level. It also achieved an 80% success rate in autonomous picking experiments combining a Vision-Language Model (VLM) and object detection, proving this whole-body control framework functions reliably in the real world rather than just in theory.
contributions: Proposed a hybrid task representation combining base-relative position and gravity-aligned orientation to balance end-effector tracking with workspace retention on uneven terrain.

Constructed a task-prioritized reinforcement learning framework with explicit dependencies among body stabilization, locomotion, and manipulation, suppressing unreasonable arm motions based on walking status.
Developed Lite Arm, an ultra-lightweight 1.5 kg 6-DoF arm to minimize payload stress on a small-scale quadruped robot, realizing a compact hardware platform with a total weight of 13.5 kg.

Demonstrated end-effector stabilization on 30-degree slopes, stairs, and soft ground, as well as autonomous grasping from natural language instructions (80% success rate), both in simulation and on real hardware.

sections.heading: Unifying the whole body with hybrid task representation and prioritized learning
sections.summary: To reconcile manipulation performance and locomotion stability on uneven terrain, the authors devised a hybrid representation that splits the reference frame between end-effector position and orientation. Furthermore, they constructed an RL reward function that prioritizes body stability, locomotion, and manipulation, ensuring lower-priority tasks do not threaten higher-priority stability.
sections.details:
### II-A System Configuration and Problem Formulation
This work targets a system consisting of a small quadruped robot (Unitree Go1) equipped with a custom 6-DoF arm named "Lite Arm" (12 leg DoFs + 6 arm DoFs = 18 DoFs total). The arm itself weighs only 1.5 kg with a maximum reach exceeding 60 cm, combining carbon-fiber-reinforced PLA parts and carbon tubes to balance rigidity and lightness. A policy controlling these 18 DoFs simultaneously (whole-body control: WBC) is learned through reinforcement learning using PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization).

### II-B Hybrid Task Representation
This is a major architectural highlight. How should the target for the end-effector (EE) be defined?
- If both position and orientation are specified in the world frame (absolute coordinates), whenever the terrain is uneven and the base pitches, rolls, or sinks significantly, the target escapes the arm's physical reachable space (workspace), hitting joint limits.
- Conversely, if specified in the robot base frame (relative coordinates), reachability improves, but climbing a 30-degree slope tilts the end-effector by 30 degrees as well, failing tasks like carrying liquids or objects horizontally.

To get the best of both worlds, the authors proposed a "hybrid representation." The target end-effector position ${}^{B}\mathbf{p}_t$ is given in the base frame to keep it consistently within reach, while the target orientation $\mathbf{q}_t$ is defined with reference to the gravity vector to align the EE z-axis with the world vertical direction. This keeps the end-effector level regardless of how much the base shakes.

### II-C Task-Prioritized Whole-Body Learning
Even with clear targets, it is counterproductive if locomotion and end-effector tracking interfere with each other during learning. Thus, a three-stage priority hierarchy based on dependencies was introduced.
1. **Priority I (Body Stability $R_{\mathrm{body}}$)**: Fall prevention is the top priority. When the base tilts away from an upright posture, the activation coefficient $\lambda_{\mathrm{upright}} \in [0, 1]$ decreases, damping the entire locomotion and manipulation reward.
2. **Priority II (Locomotion Performance $R_{\mathrm{loco}}$)**: Tracking walking velocity. If locomotion is inadequate, the coefficient $\lambda_{\mathrm{loco}} \in [0, 1]$ shrinks, dampening the manipulation contribution.
3. **Priority III (Manipulation Tracking $R_{\mathrm{mani}}$)**: Consists of coarse position tracking, fine position tracking near the target, and gravity-aligned orientation tracking.

These terms are unified via a dynamic weight vector $\mathbf{\Lambda} = [1, \lambda_{\mathrm{upright}}, \lambda_{\mathrm{upright}} \lambda_{\mathrm{loco}}]^{\top}$, computing the per-step reward $r_t^{\mathrm{pri}} = \mathbf{\Lambda}^{\top} [R_{\mathrm{body}}, R_{\mathrm{loco}}, R_{\mathrm{mani}}]^{\top}$. In short, this structure autonomously encourages the RL agent to decide: "Do not force arm movements when footing is unstable."

sections.heading: Simulation training via asymmetric actor-critic and curriculum learning
sections.summary: Training was conducted in Isaac Lab across 4096 parallel environments using PPO with an asymmetric actor-critic structure. Alongside privileged information for efficient learning, curriculum learning that progressively raises terrain difficulty and thorough domain randomization enabled zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
sections.details:
### III-A Observation and Action Spaces
Training employs an "Asymmetric Actor-Critic" architecture where the policy (actor) and value function (critic) receive different information.
- The actor's input is a 70-dimensional vector directly measurable on the real robot: joint positions (18D), joint velocities (18D), previous actions (18D), whole-body commands (linear velocity, yaw velocity + EE position and orientation, 10D), base angular velocities (3D), and projected gravity vector (3D).
- In contrast, the critic, used only during training, receives privileged information (true base linear velocity, EE acceleration, target orientation errors, and a local $17 \times 11$ elevation map under the feet), significantly stabilizing value estimation.
- The action space consists of normalized target joint positions for all 18 joints (12 leg DoFs + 6 arm DoFs).

### III-B Reward Function Design
Each term in the priority hierarchy is built from concrete physical metrics. The body term $R_{\mathrm{body}}$ penalizes unwanted collisions, swing foot clearance, foot contact forces, joint limit violations, torques, and accelerations. The locomotion term $R_{\mathrm{loco}}$ uses the standard exponential velocity tracking reward in Isaac Lab. The manipulation term $R_{\mathrm{mani}}$ includes a coarse position error penalty when far from the target, an exponentially steep fine position reward near the target, and orientation rewards aligning the EE horizontal heading (yaw) and vertical alignment (gravity direction).

### III-C Training Protocol and Sim-to-Real
Training ran at 50 Hz across 4096 parallel environments in Isaac Lab on a workstation equipped with an NVIDIA RTX 5090. Each episode lasted 1000 steps (20 seconds). Terrain difficulty was progressively scaled using curriculum learning, moving from flat ground (difficulty 0.0) to challenging terrain with height variations and obstacles (difficulty 1.0).

To ensure direct transfer to the physical robot (zero-shot sim-to-real), parameters were extensively varied (domain randomization). PD controller stiffness was scaled by 0.8–1.3x, damping by 0.5–1.5x, link masses of the arm by 1.0–1.8x, and an unknown payload mass of 0–0.5 kg was added to the end-effector. Furthermore, action latencies of 0–60 ms (up to 3 steps) and sustained disturbance forces and torques applied to the base were introduced to boost robustness.

(m) Trade-off between locomotion error and end-effector tracking error, showing the proposed method (Full) in the bottom-left corner (both errors minimized). sections.heading: From simulation ablations to real-world 30-degree slopes and autonomous picking
sections.summary: Ablations proved the three-stage priority design is essential, while real-world experiments showed the robot walking on 30-degree slopes and stairs while keeping the end-effector level. An integrated autonomous grasping pipeline with a VLM and object detector also achieved an 80% success rate on deformable terrain and descending stairs.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation Experiments and Ablations
To verify the effectiveness of the priority hierarchy, variant policies disabling each priority level were compared.
- **Disabling Locomotion Priority (Priority II)**: EE tracking error decreased, but base motion error skyrocketed. The policy prioritized arm stability over moving, making it unable to traverse uneven terrain.
- **Disabling Manipulation Priority (Priority III)**: Locomotion was maintained, but EE position error surged because the arm remained rigid in an easy, passive posture rather than actively tracking.
- **Disabling Body Stability Priority (Priority I)**: Both locomotion and manipulation collapsed. Higher-level tasks cannot function without the foundation of fall prevention.

Compared to a conventional hierarchical baseline (Hier: locomotion MPC + arm inverse kinematics), the baseline's joint torque saturation rate (frequency of exceeding 95% of the torque limit) climbed rapidly as terrain difficulty rose. In contrast, the proposed WBC distributed loads across the entire body, keeping overloading significantly lower.

### IV-B Real-World Multi-Terrain Traversal and EE Stabilization
On the real robot (Go1 + Lite Arm), the WBC policy ran on the onboard computer (NVIDIA Jetson Xavier NX) at 49.9 Hz (inference time 1.53 ms), with low-level joint control executing at 500 Hz. The robot carried a container holding two elastic balls at the end-effector as an indicator of tilt and shaking.
- **30-Degree Slopes and 10 cm Stairs**: Despite heavy base pitching, the end-effector remained almost perfectly level, successfully traversing up and down without dropping the balls. In contrast, the existing MPC baseline slipped or shook severely, causing the balls to bounce out.
- **Disturbance Rejection**: When human disturbances violently shook the base on stairs (average peak foot-plane tilt of 0.752 rad), leg coordination suppressed base tilt to 0.499 rad, and the arm compensated along the z-axis (error 0.034 m). As a result, the EE orientation error was kept to just 0.039 rad (~2.2 degrees).

### IV-C Autonomous Grasping with VLM and Failure Analysis
To prove practical utility, an autonomous picking pipeline was integrated using an external PC running a Vision-Language Model (Qwen3-VL-32B) and GroundingDINO, driven by natural language prompts (e.g., "hand me the paper cup" or "give me the electric screwdriver").
The system achieved 17/20 successes on deformable terrain covered with sandbags and sponges (soft contacts unmodeled in simulation), and 15/20 successes while descending stairs laterally, totaling 32/40 successes (80% success rate). Out of 8 failures, only 3 were caused by locomotion/control (2 loss-of-balance incidents on steep slopes, 1 desk collision). The remaining 5 failures stemmed from perception and gripper issues, such as missing transparent containers or slips during grasp. This confirmed robust loco-manipulation even on unstable footing.

The proposed method (top and middle rows) keeps the end-effector level and transports the balls despite severe base tilt, whereas the baseline MPC (bottom row) drops the balls due to violent shaking and stops on the slope.

As shown in the bottom graph, even when a human violently shakes the base (dashed and gray lines), the end-effector orientation error (orange line) remains near zero, showing legs and arm coordinating to absorb disturbances.

A variety of objects, including a transparent cup and a 600 g electric screwdriver, were tested, with only 2 falls caused by locomotion control.

sections.heading: Conclusions and what comes next
sections.summary: This RL-based whole-body control framework proves that a small quadruped manipulator can traverse complex uneven terrain while maintaining stable end-effector manipulation. Future work will target precision evaluation in motion-capture environments and extending to complex transport tasks in dynamic settings.
sections.details:
By combining a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning, this research establishes a whole-body control framework that enables a compact quadruped manipulator to manipulate stably while navigating uneven terrain. Both simulation and hardware experiments demonstrated high mobility and end-effector orientation retention under harsh conditions such as 30-degree slopes, stairs, and deformable terrain.

A key limitation acknowledged in the paper is that real-world quantitative evaluation relied on onboard sensors (IMU and joint encoder forward kinematics) because an external motion capture system could not be set up in the outdoor and complex terrain test areas. Furthermore, verification was limited to a single hardware platform (Go1 + Lite Arm), leaving cross-platform generalizability as an open question.

For future directions, the authors plan to collect large-scale loco-manipulation datasets, make further hardware refinements, and extend the framework to more complex manipulation and dynamic transport tasks in unstructured real-world environments.

takeaways: The hybrid representation—end-effector position in the base frame (local) and orientation in the gravity frame (global)—is a highly practical design pattern resolving the conflict between limited arm workspace and level tool pose.

When learning whole-body control via RL, gating lower-priority rewards based on higher-priority task performance (body stability > locomotion > manipulation) rather than simple linear summing is key to preventing collapse on uneven terrain.

As demonstrated by the 1.5 kg custom arm, mechanical lightweighting on compact quadruped robots is just as effective as algorithmic control in suppressing moments of inertia and center-of-mass shifts.
limitations: Because external motion capture could not cover the uneven terrain testing area, millimeter-level absolute tracking errors on the real robot remain estimated via onboard sensors and forward kinematics.
Experimental validation was limited to a single platform (Unitree Go1 and the custom Lite Arm); generalizability across other quadrupeds or arm geometries has not yet been directly tested.
In autonomous grasping, non-control factors such as vision misdetections on transparent objects and gripper slip accounted for the majority of task failures.
